Black powder out of the pipeline

Magnetic Filters | Santosh Magnetic Works
Overview
Clean fluid without consumables

Fine steel particles in a coolant, oil or wash liquid score slideways, block nozzles, wear pumps and spoil the surface finish. A barrier filter catches them only if its pores are small enough, and then it blocks.

A magnetic filter works by attraction. The fluid passes over high strength neodymium rods and the iron holds to them. Particles of any size are removed at full flow. Nothing is consumed. Cleaning is a wipe of the rods.
We build the range to order at our works in Mumbai, with the connection size and magnetic strength matched to your line. Every unit comes with a tested certificate of magnetic strength.
Filtration range
Where a magnetic filter pays for itself
Grinding and machining coolant lasts longer and the finish improves. Hydraulic and gear oil carries less wear metal, so the machine wears less. Wash tanks stop redepositing iron on the next batch.
Most contamination in a metalworking fluid is iron. Put the magnetic filter first and a coarser barrier filter after it, and the barrier filter lasts many times longer.

Lift steel with one person and one lever
A permanent magnetic lifter picks up a steel plate, block or round bar with no chains, slings or clamps. Set it on the load, turn the handle, and lift. Turn the handle back and the load is released.
The magnets are neodymium. There is no power supply and no battery, so the hold cannot fail in a power cut. The handle locks in the on position.

Basics guide
Back to Guides
Only a few metals are attracted to a magnet. Iron is the main one. Most other metals, such as aluminium, copper, brass and lead, are passed over by a magnet.
This guide explains which metals are magnetic, why, and what that means when you use magnets to protect a product line.
The metals a magnet will pick up
Three common metals are strongly magnetic:
Iron, and every steel made mainly from iron
Nickel
Cobalt
These are called ferromagnetic metals. A magnet pulls them with real force. A steel bolt, a nail, a piece of swarf and a broken machine part are all picked up easily.
Some rare metals are also magnetic, such as gadolinium. These are unusual in a factory and you will seldom meet them.
The metals a magnet will pass over
Most metals are not attracted to a magnet in any useful way. Common examples are:
Aluminium
Copper
Brass and bronze
Lead
Zinc
Gold and silver
Titanium
A magnet has no useful pull on these. A magnetic separator will leave them in the product. If these metals are a risk on your line, a magnet alone will not remove them.
Why some metals are magnetic

Every atom acts like a very small magnet. In most materials these small magnets point in random directions, so they cancel each other out. In iron, nickel and cobalt, the atoms line up in small groups called domains. When a magnet comes near, the domains turn to face the same way and the metal is pulled towards it.
The strength of the pull depends on how much iron the metal contains, how the metal was made, and its shape. A thin, sharp piece is pulled less strongly than a solid block of the same weight.
Stainless steel is a special case

Stainless steel is made mostly from iron, so many people expect all of it to be magnetic. Some grades are, and some are not. Grades 304 and 316, which are common in food and chemical plants, are only weakly magnetic. Grades such as 430 are strongly magnetic. See our guide {1}Are All Stainless Steels Magnetic?{/1} for the detail.

Work hardening changes this. When a 304 stainless part is cut, bent or ground, the worked area becomes weakly magnetic. A high strength separator will still catch most fine stainless particles from wear on stainless equipment.
What this means on a production line

Most metal contamination in a factory is iron or steel. It comes from worn machine parts, screens, bolts, tools and the raw material itself. A magnetic separator removes this at low cost, with no power and very little maintenance.
A SMAG neodymium separator rod in a sealed stainless steel tube.

The strength of the magnet decides how small a particle it can hold. Standard rods of 7,000 to 8,000 gauss remove ordinary tramp iron. High strength rods of 9,500 gauss and above hold fine particles and weakly magnetic stainless steel.
Aluminium, copper and brass need another method, such as a metal detector or a sieve.

Are All Stainless Steels Magnetic? | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / Are All Stainless Steels Magnetic?
Some stainless steels are magnetic and some are not. It depends on the grade. Grade 430 is strongly magnetic. Grades 304 and 316 are weakly magnetic or not magnetic at all.
This matters in food, pharmaceutical and chemical plants, where most equipment is made from stainless steel and wear particles from that equipment can end up in the product.
What stainless steel is

Stainless steel is an alloy. It is mostly iron, with at least 10.5 percent chromium. The chromium forms a thin layer on the surface that stops rust. Nickel, molybdenum, carbon and other elements are added to change the strength and the corrosion resistance.
The mix of elements changes the crystal structure of the steel. The crystal structure decides whether the steel is magnetic.
The main families of stainless steel
There are five families.

{1}Ferritic stainless steels{/1} are magnetic. They contain chromium and little or no nickel. Grades 409, 430 and 439 are ferritic. They are used in car exhausts, kitchen appliances and cheaper fittings.
{1}Martensitic stainless steels{/1} are magnetic. They contain more carbon and can be hardened. Grades 410, 420 and 440 are martensitic. Knife blades, valve parts and shafts are often made from them.

{1}Austenitic stainless steels{/1} are not magnetic in their normal state. They contain nickel, which changes the crystal structure. Grades 304 and 316 are austenitic. Most food and pharmaceutical equipment, tanks, pipes and screens are made from these grades.
{1}Duplex stainless steels{/1} are a mix of ferritic and austenitic. They are magnetic and very corrosion resistant. They are used in chemical plants and in oil and gas.
{1}Precipitation hardened stainless steels{/1} are magnetic. They are used in aerospace and in high strength parts.
Why 304 and 316 can still be caught

Austenitic steel becomes partly magnetic when it is worked. Cutting, bending, grinding and rubbing change the crystal structure in the worked area. A screen that has been vibrating for years, a blade that has been sharpened, or a pipe that has been bent will all show a weak pull.
The fine particles that wear off stainless equipment are work hardened by the wear itself. This is why a high strength magnet can remove them, even though the parent metal seems to ignore a magnet.
The pull is weak, so the magnet must be strong and the particle must pass close to it. Standard strength rods will miss most of these particles. Rods of 9,500 gauss and above hold them.
A simple test
Hold a small permanent magnet against the metal.
A firm pull means a ferritic, martensitic or duplex grade.
A weak pull, or a pull only at cut edges and welds, points to a worked austenitic grade such as 304.
No pull at all means an austenitic grade in its soft state.
A gauss meter gives a more useful measurement when you need to check the strength of a separator itself.
Choosing a separator for stainless contamination
Use the highest practical strength. SMAG rods are made in four tiers, up to 13,500 gauss.
Keep the product path close to the magnet. Grids and drawer housings space the rods so that every particle passes within a few millimetres of a rod.
Clean the rods often. A rod covered in collected iron has a weaker surface field.
Check the strength once a year with a gauss meter against the certificate supplied with the unit.

Food Safety guide

HACCP is a food safety system. The letters stand for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. The idea is simple. Find the places where a hazard can enter the food. Put a control at each place. Check the control, and write down the result.
Metal is one of the most common physical hazards in food. This guide shows how to handle it under HACCP with magnetic separation.
Step 1: find where metal can enter
Walk the whole line, starting at intake and ending at packing. At each stage, ask where iron or steel could come from. Common sources are:
{1}Raw materials.{/1} Grain, sugar, flour, spices and powders arrive with nails, wire, staples and rust flakes from harvesting, storage and transport.
{1}Sieves and screens.{/1} Wire mesh breaks and sheds fine pieces.
{1}Mills, mixers and pumps.{/1} Blades, bearings and seals wear and shed particles.
{1}Conveyors and elevators.{/1} Bolts, chain links and belt fasteners work loose.
{1}Maintenance.{/1} Swarf, filings and dropped fixings after a repair.
{1}Packaging.{/1} Staples and wire from sacks and cases.
Write each source down with the stage where it appears.
Step 2: decide which points are critical
A critical control point is a stage where a control can prevent the hazard, or reduce it to a safe level, and where no later stage will catch it. For metal, the usual critical points are:
{1}Intake{/1}, to protect your own equipment from tramp iron in the raw material.
{1}After each mill, sieve or mixer{/1}, to catch wear particles that stage creates.
{1}Before packing{/1}, as the final check on the finished product.
The final point is the most important. Anything that passes it reaches the customer.
Step 3: fit a control at each point
A magnetic separator is the usual control for iron and steel. Choose the type to suit the product flow:
A SMAG double drawer housing for an enclosed transfer line.
{1}Grids and grates{/1} for powders and granules falling through a hopper or sieve outlet.
{1}Housed drawer separators{/1} for enclosed transfer lines and pneumatic conveying.
{1}Liquid traps{/1} for syrups, oils, sauces and slurries in a pipeline.
{1}Plate and chute magnets{/1} for deep product beds on belts and in ducts.

At the final point, use the highest practical strength. SMAG rods are made up to 13,500 gauss, and at this strength they hold fine particles and work hardened stainless steel as well as ordinary iron.
For metals a magnet cannot hold, such as aluminium and copper, add a metal detector or a sieve at the same point.
Step 4: set a limit and a check
Each critical control point needs a limit and a way to check it. For a magnetic separator, the checks are:
{1}Strength.{/1} Measure the surface field with a gauss meter and compare it with the tested certificate supplied with the unit. Do this at least once a year, and after any impact or overheating.
{1}Cleaning.{/1} Clean the rods on a fixed schedule. A rod covered in collected iron holds new particles weakly. Record what is found each time.
{1}Condition.{/1} Look for cracked or worn tubes, damaged seals and loose fixings.
Write the schedule into the HACCP plan, and keep the records with it.
Step 5: keep records and review
Auditors want to see three things. That you know where metal can enter. That you have a control at each point. And that you check the control and act on the result.

Keep the certificate of magnetic strength for each separator, the cleaning log and the gauss meter readings together. Review the plan when a line changes, when a new material is introduced, and after any metal complaint.

Lifting guide

Lifting steel is one of the most dangerous jobs in a workshop. Plates are heavy, edges are sharp, and a load that slips can crush a hand or a foot. Most accidents happen while the load is being attached or set down.
A permanent magnetic lifter changes the way the job is done. This guide explains where the risks are and how a lifter removes them.
Where the accidents happen

{1}Attaching the load.{/1} With chains and slings, someone has to reach under or around the plate to fit the hooks. Fingers are trapped between the plate and the stack, and the person is standing next to a load that is about to move.
{1}Balancing the load.{/1} A plate hung from chains can tilt or swing. If one hook slips, the whole load drops.
{1}Setting the load down.{/1} The chains must be released by hand. Someone reaches under a plate that is resting on packers, or pulls a sling out from under a load that is already down.
{1}Damage.{/1} Chains and hooks scratch and dent finished surfaces. Worn or overloaded slings fail without warning.
How a magnetic lifter works

A permanent magnetic lifter is a block of neodymium magnets inside a steel body, with a handle on top. When the handle is turned to the on position, the magnetic field is directed down through the base into the steel load. When the handle is turned off, the field is switched inside the body and the load is released.
A SMAG Maxx permanent magnetic lifter. The handle turns the hold on and off.

There is no power supply and no battery. The lifter cannot lose its hold in a power cut. The hold is released only when the operator turns the handle, and the handle locks in the on position so that it cannot be knocked off.
How this makes the lift safer
{1}Nobody reaches under the load.{/1} The lifter is set on top of the plate. The operator's hands stay on the handle, above the load.
{1}The lift is from one point.{/1} The plate hangs level from a single point directly above its centre. There are no chains to tangle or slip.
{1}Release is remote from the load.{/1} The plate is set down, and the operator turns the handle to release it. There is no sling to pull out.
{1}One person does the job.{/1} The lifter is attached and released in seconds. Fewer people are near the load for less time.
{1}Clean surfaces.{/1} The base is flat and smooth. Finished plate and machined parts are lifted without marks.
Using a lifter safely
{1}Know the rating.{/1} Each lifter is rated for a flat load of a given thickness. A round bar is held at half the flat rating. The SMAG Maxx range covers 100 kg to 6,000 kg flat load.
{1}Check the thickness.{/1} A thin plate cannot carry the full magnetic field, so the hold is weaker. Each model has a minimum job thickness.
{1}Check the surface.{/1} Rust, scale, paint and an air gap reduce the hold. Clean the contact area.
{1}Check the material.{/1} Low carbon steel gives the full rating. Alloy steel, cast iron and hardened steel hold less.
{1}Check the temperature.{/1} The load should be below 80 degrees Celsius.
{1}Lift one piece at a time.{/1} Stacked plates may separate during the lift.
{1}Test before every lift.{/1} Raise the load a few centimetres and pause before moving.
{1}Inspect the base.{/1} Keep it clean and free of dents.
Every SMAG lifter is tested to three times its safe working load before it leaves the works.

Workholding guide

A magnetic chuck holds a steel workpiece on a machine table. The right chuck holds the part firmly, gives the wheel clear access, and lasts for years. The wrong chuck lets thin parts lift or leaves the work covered in swarf.
Answer these five questions before you order.
1. What shape is the machine table?
{1}Rectangular chucks{/1} fit surface grinders and milling machines. The workpiece sits flat and the wheel passes back and forth across it.
A SMAG rectangular permanent magnetic chuck for a surface grinder.
{1}Circular chucks{/1} fit rotary grinders and lathes. The poles run in rings or in radial lines, so a round part is held evenly as it turns. SMAG makes circular chucks up to 600 mm in diameter.
Match the chuck to the table. A chuck that overhangs the table cannot be clamped safely.
2. How large is the workpiece?
The chuck should be a little larger than the largest part you grind. A part that overhangs the chuck is held only on the section that touches it, and it can tip under the wheel.
Small parts have the opposite problem. A small part must sit across at least two poles, one north and one south, or the magnetic circuit is not complete and the part is held weakly.
3. Which pole pitch?
The pole pitch is the distance between the poles on the top plate.
Standard pitch
A small part sits on one pole.
The field has nowhere to close,
so the hold is weak.
Fine pitch
The same part sits across
several poles. The field closes
through it and holds it firmly.
Workpiece

A small part needs to sit across more than one pole to be held firmly.
{1}Standard pitch{/1} suits medium and large parts. The field reaches deep into the workpiece and gives a strong hold.

{1}Fine or close pitch{/1} suits small and thin parts. The poles are close together, so a small part always sits across several of them. The field is shallow, which also means less magnetism is left in a thin part after grinding.
If you grind both, choose the fine pitch. It holds small parts well and holds large parts adequately.
4. Permanent or electromagnetic?

{1}Permanent magnetic chucks{/1} use neodymium magnets inside the body. They need no power and no wiring. The operator turns a lever to switch the hold on and off. They cannot fail during a power cut, and they generate no heat. SMAG chucks use N35 grade neodymium.

{1}Electromagnetic chucks{/1} use coils. They can be very large, and the holding force can be adjusted. They need a power supply and a controller, and they warm up during a long run. Multicoil versions are built to customer sizes.
For most grinding shops, a permanent chuck is the simpler choice. Choose electromagnetic for very large plates or where variable holding force is needed.
5. How will you demagnetise?

A steel part keeps some magnetism after it leaves the chuck. It then attracts swarf, sticks to gauges and can upset later machining. A table top demagnetiser removes the residual magnetism in a few seconds. The SMAG Maxx-Demag bench unit has a 150 x 100 mm plate and runs from a 230 V single phase supply. Larger surface demagnetisers are built to order.
The SMAG Maxx-Demag table top demagnetiser.
Looking after a chuck
Keep the top plate clean and free of swarf before every job.
Wipe the plate with a light oil at the end of a shift to prevent rust.
Regrind the top plate when it wears. A thick all-metal top plate can be reground many times.
Do not strike the chuck. A crack in the top plate lets coolant into the magnets.

Stock Magnets guide
Each magnet material has its own strengths. The right choice depends on the pull you need, the space you have, the heat around the magnet and the conditions it works in.
Permanent and temporary magnets
A permanent magnet keeps its magnetism after it has been magnetised. All the materials below are permanent magnets.
A temporary magnet acts like a magnet only while it sits in a magnetic field. A piece of mild steel on a magnet is a temporary magnet. It loses most of the effect when it is taken away.
An electromagnet is a coil of wire around a steel core. It is a magnet only while current flows through the coil. The strength can be changed by changing the current.
Neodymium (NdFeB)
Neodymium magnets are made from an alloy of neodymium, iron and boron. They are also called NdFeB, neo or rare earth magnets.
SMAG neodymium disc magnets.
Neodymium is the strongest permanent magnet material. It gives the most pull in the least space, so a small neodymium magnet can do a large job.
It has two weak points. It loses strength when it gets hot, so keep standard grades below 80 degrees Celsius. It also rusts easily, so it is plated. A common plating is nickel copper nickel.
Neodymium is sold in grades such as N35 to N52. A higher number means a stronger magnet of the same size.
Samarium cobalt (SmCo)
Samarium cobalt is the other rare earth magnet material. It is a little weaker than neodymium.
It works well at higher temperatures than neodymium. It also resists corrosion much better, so it often needs no plating. It is used where a strong magnet must work in heat or in harsh conditions.
Alnico
Alnico is an alloy of aluminium, nickel and cobalt. The name comes from the first letters of each metal.
A SMAG alnico power magnet.

Alnico gives less pull than neodymium for the same size. In return it keeps its strength close to heat, and its field hardly changes over the years. This suits fixtures near welding and heat treatment, and instruments and sensors.
Alnico can lose some of its magnetism if it is placed near a strong opposing field or is knocked hard. It is often set in a steel pot, which protects it and directs its field to one face.
Alnico is made by casting or by sintering. Casting allows more complex shapes. Sintering gives better mechanical strength.
Ferrite (ceramic)
Ferrite magnets are made from iron oxide mixed with barium or strontium carbonate, then pressed and sintered. They are also called ceramic magnets.

Ferrite is the lowest cost magnet material and one of the most widely used. It resists corrosion well. It gives the least pull for its size of the materials here, so a ferrite magnet must be larger to give the same hold. It is common in motors, loudspeakers and general magnetic assemblies.

Separation guide

Iron gets into a product line in many ways. It comes in with the raw material. It wears off mills, screws and mixers. It is dropped during maintenance. A magnetic separator pulls this iron out of the product before it damages a machine or reaches a customer.
What is a magnetic separator?

A magnetic separator is a magnet placed in the path of the product. It holds iron and steel, and the clean product carries on through the process. It works on powders, granules, pellets, flakes, liquids, pastes and slurries.
A separator has no power supply and no moving parts in the magnet. The collected iron stays on the magnet until the operator cleans it off.
How does it work?
The product moves past the magnet. It may fall by gravity, be pumped, be blown through a pipe or be carried on a conveyor. On its way it passes through or over a rod, grid, grate or plate.
Powder or granules in
Grid of magnetic rods
Iron held on the rods
A grid of magnetic rods in a hopper. The product falls between the rods and the iron stays on them.
The magnetic field pulls iron particles onto the magnet face or the rod surface. They stay there. At each clean, the operator removes the magnet or opens the housing and wipes the iron away.
What types are there?
Separators fall into two groups.
A SMAG deep field magnetic plate separator for conveyors and chutes.

{1}Primary separators{/1} remove large tramp iron such as nails, bolts, nuts, wire and tool pieces. Their main job is to protect machines. They sit at intake points and on lines that carry coarse material such as pellets or flakes. Plate magnets are the usual choice here. They sit over a conveyor, in the floor of a chute or on a hinged chute door.

{1}Secondary separators{/1} remove fine iron, such as wear particles from process machinery. Their main job is to protect the product. They sit in the middle or at the end of a process. Rods, grids, drawer housings and liquid traps are the usual choice here. A grid in a sealed housing suits a closed gravity line. A liquid trap suits a pumped pipeline.
Many lines use both. A plate magnet at intake takes out the large pieces, which could bridge across the rods of a grid or damage them. A grid or housing further down takes out the fine particles.
Where can separators be installed?
Common positions include:
intake hoppers and silo outlets
before and after sieves
above and below mixers and mills
bulk tanker discharge and sack tipping stations
gravity chutes and transfer conveyors
pneumatic and vacuum lines
just before packing

A magnet at intake checks what arrives. A magnet mid-process catches wear from the plant. A magnet before packing protects the finished product. A plant with HACCP control points usually places a separator at each one.
Does the magnet type matter?

Yes. {1}Neodymium{/1} magnets, also called rare earth magnets, are the strongest material. They hold very fine iron particles. They suit food, pharmaceutical, plastics and chemical lines, where fine particles are the main risk. Rare earth rods should stay below 100 degrees Celsius.
{1}Ferrite{/1} magnets are weaker. They cost less and project a field further, so they suit coarse tramp iron and deep product beds on conveyors.

How is magnet strength checked?

Strength is given in gauss. A higher figure means a stronger field. In a separator, the magnet sits inside a stainless tube or cover, so the useful figure is the one measured on the outside of that tube or cover. Ask for this figure when you compare separators.

Can a magnet catch stainless steel?

Keep a record of what is found at each clean. A sudden rise in iron points to wear upstream.
Check the surface strength once a year with a gauss meter.
Inspect tubes and covers for dents and cracks.

How Black Powder Forms in Pipelines | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / How Black Powder Forms in Pipelines
Pipeline guide

Black powder is a common problem in steel pipelines. It forms in gas, oil, petrochemical and aviation fuel lines. It is fine iron sulphide and iron oxide, made by corrosion of the pipe wall. The particles are very small, often less than a micron across. They can travel as a dry powder, stay suspended in a liquid, or settle as a black sludge.
How does black powder form?
Carbon steel pipe corrodes when certain substances are present in the flow. The main ones are:
Rust and iron sulphide form on the wall
Particles break off and travel with the flow
Magnetic filter holds the black powder
Clean flow
Black powder forms on the pipe wall, travels with the flow and is held in a magnetic filter.
water
oxygen
hydrogen sulphide
carbon dioxide
Together they attack the inside of the pipe. Iron from the wall reacts to form iron sulphide and iron oxide. These compounds break away from the wall as fine particles and join the flow.
The process is slow. Over months and years, an untreated line can collect a large amount of black powder. The flow also rubs against the pipe wall, and this erosion adds more particles.
Why is black powder a problem?
{1}It narrows the pipe.{/1} Black powder settles along the pipe and at low points. The open bore gets smaller, so flow and pressure fall. Operators then have to scrape or pig the line to clear it.

{1}It wears equipment.{/1} The particles are hard and abrasive. They wear the pipe wall and damage compressors, pumps, valves and burner nozzles. They can also block small passages. A meter with black powder in it can give false readings.

{1}It blocks barrier filters.{/1} Many lines use cartridge or barrier filters to catch black powder. The fine particles soon block them. Each blocked filter has to be removed, replaced and disposed of. This brings a steady cost in filter elements, labour and waste handling.
{1}It is hazardous to handle.{/1} Dry iron sulphide can catch fire on contact with air. Used filters and collected powder need careful handling and must be disposed of as hazardous waste.
How does a magnetic filter help?

Black powder is an iron compound, so a magnet holds it. A magnetic pipeline filter places strong neodymium rods in the flow. As gas or liquid passes the rods, the particles collect on them. The clean flow carries on down the line.

A magnetic filter has no filter element to block or replace. The flow path stays open as the rods load, so pressure stays steady between cleans. To clean the filter, the rods are lifted out and wiped. The collected powder is removed in one place, in a controlled way.
With a magnetic filter upstream, barrier filters further down the line block less often. Compressors, pumps, valves and meters see less abrasive wear.
Where do the filters go?
Filters can be fitted at many points in the system:
Upstream, at wellhead control, heating and cooling systems and pressure reduction.
Midstream, in filtration trains, gas gathering stations and pig receiving stations.
Downstream, at refinery inlets and storage.
Ahead of compressors, meters and control valves anywhere in the line.
Sizing a filter

To size a filter, we need the line size, the operating pressure, the flow rate and the type of contamination you see. The connection type matters too, because each unit is made to fit the existing pipework.

How Magnetic Filtration Works | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / How Magnetic Filtration Works
Filtration guide

Magnetic filtration removes iron and steel particles from a liquid with a magnet. The liquid flows around magnetic rods. The particles are pulled onto the rods and stay there. The clean liquid carries on to the machine or the next stage of the process.
It is used for machine coolant, cutting fluid, neat oil, hydraulic oil, wash liquid and many process liquids.
What is inside the filter?
A magnetic filter has two main parts: a housing and a set of magnetic rods.
Magnetic rods of this kind sit inside the filter housing.
The housing is a sealed body with an inlet and an outlet. It fits into the pipe that carries the liquid. The rods hang inside the housing, in the path of the flow.

Each rod is a sealed stainless steel tube. Inside the tube are strong neodymium magnets with steel pole pieces between them. The pole pieces concentrate the magnetic field at the surface of the tube. The tube is welded and watertight, so the liquid never touches the magnets.
How are the particles caught?
Iron and steel are ferrous metals. A magnet attracts them.
Liquid with iron particles
Magnetic rods hold the iron
Sealed housing
Lid lifts out with
the rods for cleaning
Liquid flows around the magnetic rods. Iron particles are pulled onto the rods and the clean liquid flows on.

As the liquid passes the rods, each ferrous particle feels a pull towards the nearest rod. The pull is strongest close to the rod surface. A particle that comes close enough is drawn onto the tube and held there. The flow is not strong enough to wash it off.

Size does not decide what is caught. A large chip and a very fine grinding particle are both ferrous, so both are attracted. This is why a magnetic filter can hold the fine wear particles that pass through a paper or bag filter. The page on {1}magnetic filters compared with other filters{/1} sets out the differences in full.
Some non-magnetic dirt is also held. It gets trapped in the layer of iron that builds up on the rods. The amount depends on the liquid and the process.
What decides how well it works?

{1}Magnetic strength.{/1} Strength at the rod surface is measured in gauss. A stronger rod reaches further into the flow and holds finer particles. SMAG rods are made in four strengths, from 7,000 gauss up to 13,500 gauss.

{1}Time near the rods.{/1} The liquid must pass close to the rods and slowly enough for the particles to be drawn out. The housing is sized to the flow rate for this reason. The rods are spaced so that the liquid cannot find a path that avoids them.
{1}Amount of iron.{/1} A heavy load of swarf fills the rods faster. More rods, a larger housing or more frequent cleaning deal with a heavy load.
{1}Temperature.{/1} Neodymium magnets lose strength if they get too hot. Rare earth rods should stay below 100 degrees Celsius.
Does the filter block?

The rods sit in the flow with open space around them. The liquid passes through that space. As iron builds up on the rods, the liquid still has a clear path, so the flow to the machine stays steady and there is no pressure build-up.
A full rod collects less, though. Clean the rods before the layer of iron gets thick.
Where does it go in the line?

Fit the magnetic filter where the dirty liquid returns from the machine, before it goes back to the tank or on to any other filter. The magnet then takes out the iron first. Any bag, paper or cartridge filter after it receives less dirt and lasts longer.
Fit the filter with enough space above it to lift the rods out.
How do you clean it?
Stop the flow or divert it.
Open the lid of the housing.
Lift the rod assembly out.
Wipe or scrape the iron off the rods with a cloth or a plastic scraper.
Refit the rods and close the lid.
The collected iron comes off as a damp paste of metal. There is no filter bag or paper to throw away. The magnets keep their strength for many years, so the same rods go back in each time.
How often to clean depends on the amount of iron in the liquid. Check the rods daily at first. Once you know how fast they load, set a regular cleaning time.
Checking the rods
Look for scratches or dents in the stainless tube. A damaged tube can let liquid reach the magnets. Replace a damaged rod.
A {1}gauss meter{/1} measures the strength at the rod surface. Compare the reading with the certificate supplied with the rod.

How to Keep Machine Coolant Clean for Longer | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / How to Keep Machine Coolant Clean for Longer
Machine coolant wears out. Tramp oil, bacteria, metal fines and the wrong mix all shorten its life. Most of these can be controlled with good habits. Start by keeping dirt out of the coolant.
Remove tramp oil
Tramp oil is oil that leaks into the coolant from the machine. It comes from slideways, gearboxes and hydraulic systems. It floats on top of the coolant in the sump.
A layer of tramp oil keeps air away from the coolant. Bacteria grow under it, and the coolant starts to smell. Tramp oil also marks the parts and reduces cooling.
Remove it with a disc or belt skimmer, or with a coalescing separator. Fix the leaks that let it in.
Filter out metal fines
Fine metal from cutting and grinding stays in the coolant and goes round the machine again and again. It scratches parts, wears tools and pumps, and turns into sludge in the sump.
Choose a filter to suit the metal you cut:
A {1}magnetic filter{/1} holds iron and steel particles, including very fine ones. It does not catch aluminium, brass or other non-ferrous metals.
A {1}barrier filter{/1}, such as a bag, paper or cartridge filter, holds any particle larger than its pores. Some fine barrier filters also take out part of the additives in the coolant.

On mixed work, use both. Put the magnetic filter first. It takes out the iron, so the barrier filter after it fills more slowly and lasts longer. {1}Magnetic filters compared with other filters{/1} explains the difference in detail.
Clean the magnetic rods before they are heavily loaded.
Check the concentration
Coolant is a concentrate mixed with water. The mix must be right.
{1}Too weak{/1}, and the coolant lubricates less, protects less against rust and lets bacteria grow.
{1}Too strong{/1}, and it can irritate the operator's skin. It also wastes concentrate.
Check the concentration once a week with a refractometer. Adjust the mix to the level the coolant maker gives.
Top up the right way
Coolant evaporates, and the water goes first. Top up with coolant that is already mixed to the right strength. Plain water from the tap lowers the concentration and helps bacteria grow.
Water with a lot of minerals leaves deposits in the machine. Reverse osmosis or deionised water avoids this.
When mixing, always add the concentrate to the water. Never mix two different coolants. They can react with each other and make the coolant unstable.
Keep the sump clean
Swarf, chips and sludge settle in the sump. Bacteria grow in them, and sludge can block the pump.
Remove chips and swarf from the sump regularly.
When you change the coolant, empty the sump fully and clean out all the sludge.
Flush the system with a system cleaner before the new fill.
Keep the coolant moving

Coolant that stands still in an idle machine goes bad faster. Bacteria grow when there is no flow and no air. Run the pump for a while each day, or use aeration, when a machine stands for a long time.
Stop coolant from smelling
A bad smell means bacteria are growing. To stop it:
Remove the tramp oil.
Filter out the metal fines.
Keep the concentration correct.
Keep the coolant moving when the machine is idle.
How often should coolant be changed?

With good habits, one fill of coolant can last many months. Without them, it may need changing after a few weeks. The life also depends on the machine, the metal being cut and how many hours the machine runs.
Watch for these signs that it is time to change:
a bad smell
foaming
a thick layer of tramp oil
sludge that returns soon after cleaning
Store coolant concentrate safely
Keep containers sealed.
Keep them out of direct sun, frost and great heat.
Label every container clearly.
Use clean mixing equipment that is kept only for coolant.
Keep the store clean and away from other chemicals.

{1}Guides{/1} / What to Check Before Using a Magnetic Lifter
A permanent magnetic lifter is simple to use. Set it on the load, turn the handle, and lift. The hold depends on the load as much as on the lifter, so a few checks are needed before every lift.
This guide lists them in order.
1. Is the load within the rating?

Every lifter has a safe working load for a flat plate of low carbon steel, at a given minimum thickness, with a clean flat surface. This is the flat rating. A round bar touches the base along a single line, so the round rating is half the flat rating.
Know the weight of the load. If you are not sure, work it out from the size. A steel plate weighs about 7.85 kg for every square metre of area per millimetre of thickness.
2. Is the plate thick enough?

The magnetic field passes into the load. A thin plate cannot carry the whole field, and some of it passes through to the other side. The hold is weaker. Each SMAG Maxx model has a minimum job thickness, from 15 mm on the smallest to 100 mm on the largest. Below that thickness, the rated load is reduced.
Plate thick enough
The field closes inside the plate.
The lifter holds its full rating.
Plate too thin
Part of the field passes through
the plate into the air.
The hold is weaker.
A thin plate cannot carry the whole field, so the lifter holds less.
3. Is the contact surface clean and flat?

The hold falls quickly with any gap between the base and the load. Rust, scale, paint, oil, swarf and a rough surface all count as a gap. Clean the contact area before the lift. A machined or ground surface gives the full rating.
4. What is the load made of?
Low carbon steel gives the full rating. Other materials hold less:
Medium carbon and alloy steels hold a little less.
Cast iron holds roughly half.
Hardened steel holds less than soft steel of the same grade.
Austenitic stainless steel, aluminium, copper and brass are not held at all.
5. How hot is the load?
Heat weakens the magnets. Keep the load below 80 degrees Celsius. Do not lift material straight from a furnace or a hot cutting process.
6. Is the load one piece?

Lift one plate at a time. Two stacked plates may seem to lift together, then separate in the air. Long thin plates may sag at the ends and peel away from the base. Place the lifter over the centre of gravity.
7. Is the lifter in good condition?
Look at the base. It should be clean, flat and free of dents and swarf. Check that the handle turns fully and locks in the on position. Check the shackle and the crane hook.
8. Test the lift
Raise the load a few centimetres. Pause. Check that the load is level and holding. Then move it, keeping it low and clear of people.
After the lift

Set the load down fully before turning the handle off. Turn the handle to the off position and lift the lifter clear. Never leave the lifter switched on with no load. Store it on a wooden or non-magnetic surface.

{1}Guides{/1} / Magnetic Filters Compared with Other Filters

Most industrial filters work by blocking. The fluid passes through a mesh, a paper, a bag or a cartridge, and the particles are held back. A magnetic filter works by attraction. The fluid passes over magnets, and iron particles are pulled out of the flow and held on the magnet surface.
This guide compares the two approaches for coolants, oils, wash liquids and process fluids.
How a magnetic filter works

A magnetic filter is a housing fitted into a pipeline. Inside are one or more high strength magnetic rods. Fluid enters, passes over and around the rods, and leaves. Iron and steel particles in the fluid are drawn to the rods and held there.
A SMAG inline magnetic liquid trap.
The rods are cleaned by lifting them out of the housing and wiping off the collected material. Nothing is consumed. The magnets keep their strength for many years.
What each type catches

{1}Bag, cartridge and paper filters{/1} catch anything larger than their pore size. They catch iron, aluminium, plastic, dirt and fibres alike. They cannot catch anything smaller than the pore size, and a very fine filter blocks quickly and restricts the flow.
{1}Magnetic filters{/1} catch iron and steel of any size, down to particles of a few microns, with no restriction to the flow. They do not catch aluminium, brass, plastic or dirt.
In practice, most contamination in a metalworking or steel processing fluid is iron. A magnetic filter removes that, and a coarser barrier filter handles the rest.

Non-magnetic contamination needs a barrier. Aluminium and brass swarf, plastic, fibres and general dirt pass over a magnet. In a system with mixed contamination, fit the magnetic filter first. It removes the bulk of the load, so the barrier filter downstream lasts far longer and can be coarser.

{1}Guides{/1} / Preventing Product Recalls in the Food Industry

A product recall is one of the most costly events a food business can face. The product must be traced, collected and destroyed. Sales stop. Retailers lose confidence. The story may reach the press. Recovery can take years.
Many recalls are avoidable. This guide looks at the common causes and the controls that prevent them, with a focus on metal.
Why food is recalled
The main reasons for food recalls are:
{1}Undeclared allergens{/1}, such as milk, nuts or gluten missing from the label.
{1}Microbiological contamination{/1}, such as salmonella or listeria.
{1}Physical contamination{/1}, mostly metal, glass and plastic.
Labelling and packaging errors.
{1}Chemical contamination{/1}, such as cleaning agents or excess additives.
Physical contamination is the category where engineering controls do most of the work. Metal is the largest part of it.
What a recall costs

The direct costs are the product, the logistics of collecting it, disposal, and the staff time spent managing the event. The indirect costs are larger. Lost sales during and after the recall, penalties from retailers, legal claims, higher insurance and the long term damage to the brand.
A single high strength magnetic separator costs a small fraction of a single recall.
Control 1: know your hazards

Under HACCP, every plant must list the hazards at each stage and decide where they must be controlled. For metal, walk the line and write down where iron and steel can enter. Raw materials, sieves, mills, mixers, pumps, conveyors and maintenance work are the usual sources. See our guide on {1}critical control points{/1}
Control 2: remove metal at every stage

Fit a magnetic separator at intake, after each stage that sheds metal, and before packing. Use a grid or grate for powders in a hopper, a drawer housing for enclosed lines, a liquid trap for pipelines and a plate or chute magnet for deep beds.
A SMAG housed liquid trap for syrup, oil and sauce lines.

The final separator before packing is the last chance to catch a fragment. Use the highest practical strength here. SMAG rods are made up to 13,500 gauss, which holds fine particles and work hardened stainless steel as well as ordinary iron.
Control 3: cover the metals a magnet passes

Aluminium, copper, brass and some stainless grades are passed by a magnet. If these are a risk on your line, add a metal detector after the final magnet. The magnet removes the bulk of the contamination and protects the detector from constant rejects. The detector catches the remainder.
Control 4: prove the controls work
An auditor wants evidence. For each separator, keep:
The {1}tested certificate of magnetic strength{/1} supplied when it was made.
A {1}cleaning log{/1} showing when it was cleaned and what was found.
{1}Gauss meter readings{/1} taken at least once a year, compared with the certificate.
An {1}inspection record{/1} for tube damage, seal wear and loose fixings.
A separator with no records is treated as no control at all.
Control 5: manage change

Recalls often follow a change. A new supplier, a new product, a repair or a new machine. Review the hazard list and the separator positions every time the line changes, and after every metal complaint, even if the complaint is not confirmed.
Control 6: train the people

Operators must know how to clean a separator, what to record, and what to do when they find more metal than usual. Maintenance staff must know to count tools and fixings, and to clean with a hand magnet before a restart.

{1}Guides{/1} / Reducing Metal Contamination in Food Processing

Metal in food is a serious hazard. A single fragment can injure a customer, trigger a recall and damage a brand for years. Most of that metal is iron or steel, and most of it can be removed with magnets.
This guide gives the practical steps that reduce the risk.
Where the metal comes from
Metal enters a food line in three ways.

{1}It arrives with the raw material.{/1} Grain, sugar, flour, salt, spices, cocoa and dried fruit come from farms, mills and warehouses. Along the way they pick up nails, wire, staples, rust and pieces of broken equipment.

{1}The line makes it.{/1} Every moving part wears. Mill blades, sieve mesh, mixer paddles, pump rotors, conveyor chains and bearings shed particles as they run. Stainless steel equipment sheds stainless particles.
{1}People bring it.{/1} Dropped fixings after maintenance, a broken blade, swarf from a repair, a paperclip or a pen spring.
What it costs

A recall in the food industry costs far more than the product itself. There is the cost of finding and collecting the product, the lost sales, the legal exposure and the loss of trust from retailers and consumers. Metal is one of the most common causes of recalls worldwide.
Retailer audits treat metal control as a basic requirement. A line with no magnetic protection, or with separators that are never checked, will fail.
Step 1: protect the intake

Fit a magnetic separator where raw material enters the plant. A grate magnet in the intake hopper, or a plate magnet over the first conveyor, removes the large tramp iron. This protects your own mills and sieves from damage as well as protecting the product.
Step 2: catch what the line creates

Fit a separator after every stage that can shed metal. After a mill or a sieve, a grid or a drawer housing catches wear particles before they travel further. In liquid lines, a magnetic trap after the pump does the same job.
The particles created by the line are small. Standard strength magnets miss many of them. Use high strength rods of 9,500 gauss and above at these points.
Step 3: check the finished product

The last separator before packing is the most important. Everything that passes it goes to the customer. Use the highest practical strength here, and place the magnet where the product flow is thin and slow so that every particle passes close to a rod.
A SMAG magnetic sampling probe for spot checks on sacks and bins.
A magnet holds iron, steel and work hardened stainless steel. It will pass aluminium, copper and brass. If those metals are a risk, add a metal detector after the final magnet.
Step 4: clean and check the magnets
A separator only works while it is clean and strong.
Clean on a fixed schedule. Easy clean designs let an operator strip the collected iron in a minute without tools.
Record what is found. A sudden increase points to a failing part upstream.
Measure the strength once a year with a gauss meter, and compare with the certificate supplied with the unit.
Replace rods that are dented, cracked or leaking.
Step 5: control maintenance work
Most large metal fragments come from maintenance. Count tools and fixings out and back in. Clean the area with a hand magnet before restarting. Inspect sieve mesh after any work nearby.

Types of Filtration for CNC Machines | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / Types of Filtration for CNC Machines

A CNC machine uses cutting fluid or coolant to cool the tool, lubricate the cut and wash away chips. The fluid picks up metal particles, dirt and sludge as it circulates. A filter removes them so the fluid goes back to the machine clean.
Dirty fluid wears tools, spoils the surface finish and damages pumps and slideways. The type of filter decides what is removed and how much work the filter needs.
Paper filters

A paper filter uses a roll or sheets of filter paper. The fluid passes through the paper. Particles larger than the pores stay on the surface. When the paper is loaded, fresh paper is fed in or the sheet is changed.
Strengths
Low cost to buy.
Easy to find, in many sizes and grades.
Limits
The paper is used up quickly on a busy machine, so it is changed often.
It can block in heavy work, and it can tear and let dirt through.
Particles smaller than the pores pass through.
Used paper goes to waste, wet with fluid and metal.
Cartridge filters
A cartridge filter uses a cylinder of filter material. The material can be paper, fabric or metal mesh. The fluid passes through the wall of the cartridge and the dirt stays behind.
Lasts longer than paper, so it is changed less often.
Catches a wide range of particle sizes.
Many filter materials are available to suit the job.
Costs more to buy than a paper filter.
Elements must be cleaned or replaced.
A dense cartridge makes the pump work harder.
Used cartridges add to waste, and some materials cannot be recycled.
Bag filters
A bag filter is a bag of filter cloth held in a housing. The fluid flows into the bag and out through the cloth. The bag holds a large amount of dirt before it is full.
Holds a lot of dirt, so it suits heavy contamination.
Low running cost where there is a lot of coarse dirt.
Less good at holding fine particles.
The cloth can tear under hard use.
Used bags go to waste.
Centrifugal filters

A centrifuge spins the fluid at high speed. The spinning force throws the solid particles outwards, where they collect. The clean fluid is taken from the centre. A centrifuge separates particles by their density, so it can remove very small particles.
No filter media to buy or replace.
Removes a wide range of particle sizes, both ferrous and non-ferrous.
High cost to buy.
It is a machine with moving parts. Rotors and seals wear, need servicing and can fail.
Less suited to very large volumes of fluid.
It can warm the fluid as it runs.
Magnetic filters

A magnetic filter passes the fluid over strong magnetic rods. Iron and steel particles are pulled onto the rods and held. The clean fluid flows on. To clean the filter, lift the rods out, wipe off the iron and put them back. {1}How magnetic filtration works{/1} explains this in more detail.
Neodymium magnetic rods of the kind used in a SMAG magnetic filter.
Some non-magnetic dirt also gets caught in the layer of iron on the rods.
Holds very fine ferrous particles.
The open path past the rods does not block, so the flow stays steady and there is no pressure build-up.
Nothing to replace. The rods are cleaned and used again.
Needs no power to run.
The iron comes off the rods as metal that can be sold as scrap.
Removes only ferrous particles. Aluminium, brass, plastic and general dirt pass through.
Costs more to buy than a simple paper or bag filter.

What Does a Coolant Filter Do? | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / What Does a Coolant Filter Do?
A coolant filter takes dirt out of the coolant as it circulates round a machine. The coolant goes back to the cutting area clean, so it can do its job.
What does coolant do?
Coolant is sprayed onto the tool and the workpiece while the machine cuts or grinds. It does three jobs:
It carries heat away from the cutting area.
It lubricates the tool as it cuts.
It washes chips and swarf away from the work.
After that, the coolant runs back to a tank, often called the sump. A pump sends it round again. The same coolant can circulate for months.
What gets into the coolant?
Every pass through the machine adds dirt:
fine metal particles from grinding, honing and cutting
small chips that the chip conveyor misses
wear particles from the machine itself
sludge, a mix of fine metal, broken-down coolant and dirt
tramp oil that leaks from slideways and hydraulic systems
On machines that work steel or cast iron, most of the solid dirt is ferrous. Much of it is very fine.
What happens if the coolant is dirty?
Dirt in the coolant goes back to the cutting area on the next pass. There it causes damage:
Particles scratch the surface of the part and spoil the finish.
Parts can move out of tolerance, and more parts are rejected.
The tool and the grinding wheel wear faster.
Nozzles and small coolant lines block.
Pumps, seals and slideways wear.
Sludge builds up in the sump and bacteria grow in it. The coolant starts to smell and breaks down sooner.
Dirty coolant also cools less well. The tool runs hotter and wears faster.
What does a filter change?
A coolant filter removes the dirt before the coolant goes back to the machine. The results are simple:
The finish on the part is better and more even.
Fewer parts are rejected.
Tools and wheels last longer.
The machine has fewer breakdowns and repairs.
The coolant lasts longer, so it is changed less often and less is thrown away.
Clean coolant also flows at a steady rate and keeps a steady temperature. That helps close tolerance work such as grinding and deep hole drilling.
Which filter?

There are several kinds of coolant filter. Bag, paper and cartridge filters hold back particles larger than their pores. Centrifuges spin the dirt out. Magnetic filters pull iron and steel out of the flow. The guide to {1}types of filtration for CNC machines{/1} explains each one.

On machines that work steel or cast iron, a magnetic filter is a good first stage. It holds very fine ferrous particles, it does not block, and it has no filter element to replace. Where there is also aluminium, brass or other non-magnetic dirt, a barrier filter after the magnet catches the rest. For a side-by-side view, see {1}magnetic filters compared with other filters{/1}
The right system depends on the particle size, the type of coolant, the flow rate and the amount of work the machine does.
Where are coolant filters used?
{1}Grinding.{/1} Grinding makes very fine steel particles. They are the main cause of a poor finish.
{1}Bearing and precision part making.{/1} Tight tolerances need clean coolant on every pass.
{1}Machining centres and lathes.{/1} Fine swarf blocks nozzles and wears pumps.
{1}Honing and lapping.{/1} The finish depends on the coolant or oil being clean.
{1}Wire cut machines.{/1} The fluid needs to stay clean for a steady cut.
{1}Parts washers.{/1} Iron in the wash liquid settles back onto the next batch of parts.

What Is a Pot Magnet? | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / What Is a Pot Magnet?
A pot magnet is a magnet set inside a steel cup. The cup is also called the pot or the shell. Only one face of the magnet is open, and that face does the holding.
Pot magnets hold jigs, fixtures, sensors, guards, signs and tools. They also hang cables and hoses from steel frames.
How the steel cup works
A bare magnet has a field on every side. Most of that field goes into the air and does no work.
A bare magnet
The field spreads out on every side.
Only part of it reaches the steel.
A pot magnet
The steel cup carries the field
to the face. It closes through the
steel and the hold is much stronger.
Cup
Magnet
The steel cup brings the field to the working face, where it closes through the steel.

The steel cup collects the field from the back of the magnet. It carries the field round to the working face. The magnet forms one pole in the centre of the face. The rim of the cup forms the other pole around it. The field only has a short distance to travel between the two poles, through the steel you are holding.
This makes the pull on the working face several times what the bare magnet gives. It also puts the hold on one face only, so the back and sides of the pot do not grab nearby steel.
Protection for the magnet
Magnet materials are hard and brittle. They can chip or crack if they are knocked.

In a pot magnet, the steel cup takes the knocks. A well made pot sets the magnet face a little below the rim, so any blow lands on the steel. The cup also keeps dirt and moisture away from most of the magnet.
Fixings
A magnet on its own is too brittle to drill or thread. The steel cup can be drilled and threaded, so a pot magnet can be bolted to a fixture.
Common fixings are:
a plain back, for fitting into a recess or bonding in place
a threaded stud or a threaded hole
a countersunk hole for a screw
a hook, for hanging cables, hoses and signs
What reduces the pull
A pot magnet is rated by its pull. The rated pull is measured on thick, clean, flat mild steel with full contact. In the works the pull is often lower. These things reduce it:
{1}Thin steel.{/1} Thin plate cannot carry the whole field, so the pull drops. Use more pots, or smaller pots, on thin sheet.
{1}Air gaps.{/1} Paint, rust, dirt, scale and a curved surface all hold the magnet away from the steel. Even a small gap reduces the pull a great deal.
{1}Poor steel.{/1} Cast iron and some alloy steels carry the field less well than mild steel.
{1}Sliding load.{/1} A magnet resists a straight pull best. It slides more easily than it lifts off. Where the load pulls sideways, add a stop or a lip for the magnet to rest against.
Keep the working face and the steel clean. A pot magnet works best in direct contact.
Shallow or deep

{1}Shallow pot magnets{/1} are low and flat. They suit thin plate and fixtures where height is limited. SMAG makes shallow pots with plain, threaded, countersunk or hook fittings. One example size is 25 mm diameter by 8 mm thick.
SMAG alnico pot magnets.

{1}Deep pot magnets{/1} hold a taller magnet in a deeper steel shell. The field reaches further into the steel, so the pull on thick steel is higher than a shallow pot of the same diameter gives. They suit heavier clamping, jigs and tooling on steel frames. SMAG makes deep pots with plain, threaded or hook fittings.
Magnets near heat

SMAG pot magnets use an alnico core. Alnico is an alloy of aluminium, nickel and cobalt. It keeps its strength close to heat, and SMAG shallow pots are suited to heat up to 450 degrees Celsius. This makes alnico pots a good choice for fixtures near welding and heat treatment.

Where Are Magnets Used in Industry? | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / Where Are Magnets Used in Industry?
Magnets do four main jobs in a factory. They remove iron from a product. They hold parts still while they are worked on. They lift steel. And they clean up.
This guide describes each job in plain terms, and names the type of magnet used for it.
Removing iron from a product

Raw materials pick up iron on their way to a factory. Screws, wire, rust flakes, wear particles and pieces of broken machinery all end up in the flow. A magnetic separator pulls this iron out before it damages a machine or reaches a customer.
The magnet is chosen to suit the way the product moves:
{1}Grids and grates{/1} sit in a hopper or above a sieve. Dry powders and granules fall through the rods.
{1}Drawer housings{/1} are fitted into a pipe or a chute. The product passes over two or more rows of rods, and the drawers slide out for cleaning.
{1}Liquid traps{/1} are fitted into a pipeline. Liquids, oils and slurries pass over a bundle of rods inside a sealed housing.
{1}Plate magnets{/1} are mounted above a belt or inside a chute. They collect larger pieces of iron from a deep product bed.
{1}Chute magnets{/1} are hinged plates fitted into a sloping duct.
These separators use permanent magnets. They need no power and no maintenance beyond cleaning.
Holding parts while they are worked

A magnetic chuck holds a steel workpiece flat on a grinding machine or a lathe. The operator turns a lever and the part is locked to the table. There are no clamps to get in the way of the wheel, so the whole surface can be ground in one pass.

Rectangular chucks are used on surface grinders. Circular chucks are used on rotary grinders and lathes. After grinding, the part keeps a little magnetism. A table top demagnetiser removes it in a few seconds.
Small pot magnets and power magnets do the same job on a smaller scale. They hold jigs, guards, sensors and fixtures in place, and can be moved without tools.
Lifting steel

A permanent magnetic lifter picks up a steel plate, block or round bar with no chains or slings. The operator sets the lifter on the load, turns the handle to switch it on, and the crane does the rest. One person can move a heavy plate in seconds, and the load can be set down on a stack without anyone reaching under it.
Lifters are rated by the flat load they hold. The SMAG Maxx range covers 100 kg to 6,000 kg.
Cleaning up

A magnetic sweeper is a bar of magnets on wheels, or on a handle. It is pushed over a floor, a yard or a car park and picks up nails, screws, swarf and wire. A release lever drops the load into a bin. Sweepers protect tyres and feet, and save the time spent picking up by hand.
A SMAG magnetic sweeper picks up swarf, nails and screws from the floor.
Hand held magnetic rods do the same job in a small space. They are also used to check a product sample for iron.
Measuring magnets

A gauss meter measures the strength of a magnet at its surface. It is used to check that a separator still meets its certificate, and to compare one magnet with another. Every SMAG separator is supplied with a tested certificate, and a gauss meter is the tool for checking against it.
A gauss meter measures the strength of a magnet.

Magnetic Lifters Compared with Chains and Slings | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / Magnetic Lifters Compared with Chains and Slings
Chains and slings have moved steel for a hundred years. They work, and every workshop has them. A permanent magnetic lifter does the same job faster, with fewer people and less damage.
This guide compares the two for lifting steel plate, block and round bar.
Time per lift

{1}Chains and slings.{/1} The operator finds the right slings, walks to the load, fits the hooks or wraps the slings, checks the balance, lifts, moves, sets down on packers, and then releases and recovers the slings. A single plate can take several minutes.

{1}Magnetic lifter.{/1} The lifter stays on the crane hook. The operator lowers it onto the plate, turns the handle, lifts, moves, sets down and turns the handle again. A plate is moved in well under a minute.
Over a shift, the saving adds up to hours.
People per lift
{1}Chains and slings.{/1} Large plates usually need two people, one at each end to fit and release the slings and to steady the load.
{1}Magnetic lifter.{/1} One person operates the lifter and the crane. The second person is free for other work.
Damage to the load
{1}Chains and slings.{/1} Chains scratch and dent. Wire rope slings leave marks. Finished plate, ground surfaces and coated material must be protected with padding, which takes more time.
{1}Magnetic lifter.{/1} The base is flat and smooth. It leaves no mark on a finished surface.
Safety
{1}Chains and slings.{/1} Someone must reach under or around the load to fit and release the slings. Loads can tilt or swing. Slings wear and fail.

{1}Magnetic lifter.{/1} Hands stay on top of the load. The plate hangs level from a single point. The handle locks in the on position. There is no wear item that can fail without warning. See our guide on {3}safer lifting{/3}
Space and storage
{1}Chains and slings.{/1} A range of lengths and ratings has to be stored, inspected and tagged.
{1}Magnetic lifter.{/1} One unit covers every plate within its rating. It hangs on the crane hook.
Where chains and slings are still needed

A magnetic lifter holds only steel and iron. It will not lift aluminium, stainless steel of the austenitic grades, timber or bundles. It holds less on thin plate, on rough or painted surfaces, and on hardened or alloy steel. It is not suitable for hot material above 80 degrees Celsius.
For those loads, slings remain the right tool. For flat and round steel within its rating, the lifter is faster and safer.

Magnetic Separation for HACCP and Supplier Audits | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / Magnetic Separation for HACCP and Supplier Audits

Food manufacturers are audited by their customers and by certification bodies. The audit checks that the plant controls its hazards. Metal is a physical hazard on almost every line, so metal control is on almost every audit.
This guide explains what auditors look for and how magnetic separation meets the requirement.
Who audits, and against what

Large retailers and food service groups audit their suppliers. Certification schemes such as BRCGS, FSSC 22000 and IFS audit against published standards. In India, FSSAI requires a food safety management system based on HACCP.
All of these expect a hazard analysis, controls at the critical points, checks on those controls and records of the checks. The wording differs. The expectation is the same.
What the auditor looks for
{1}A hazard analysis that names metal.{/1} The plan should say where iron and steel can enter the product and which stages control it.

{1}Physical controls in the right places.{/1} The auditor will walk the line and look for separators at intake, after stages that shed metal, and before packing. A gap between the last separator and the packing machine is a common finding.
{1}Controls that are strong enough.{/1} Fine particles and work hardened stainless steel need high strength rods. An auditor may ask for the gauss rating and the certificate.
{1}Evidence that the controls are checked.{/1} Cleaning logs, strength readings and inspection records. A separator with no records is treated as no control.
{1}Action when something is found.{/1} If cleaning shows an unusual amount of metal, the plan should say what happens next. Stop the line, inspect upstream, check the sieve.
How magnetic separation meets each point
{1}Naming the hazard.{/1} Iron and steel from raw materials, wear and maintenance are well understood. Write them into the plan at each stage.
{1}Placement.{/1} Grids in hoppers, drawer housings in transfer lines, liquid traps in pipelines, plate and chute magnets on belts and ducts, and a final high strength unit before packing.
{1}Strength.{/1} SMAG rods are made in four tiers, up to 13,500 gauss. The rating is stated on the tested certificate supplied with each unit.
{1}Checks.{/1} Clean on a schedule and record what is found. Measure the surface field with a gauss meter at least once a year and compare with the certificate. Inspect the tubes and seals.
{1}Action.{/1} Keep the collected metal from each clean in a labelled bag until the record is reviewed. An increase in quantity or a new type of fragment points to a failing part upstream.
Sampling and verification

Some auditors ask for proof that the product after the final separator is clean. A magnetic sampling probe is pushed into a sack, a bin or a flow of product and drawn out. Any iron on the probe shows that the upstream control has missed something. Recording a clean probe at a set frequency gives positive evidence that the controls work.
A gauss meter reading checks each magnet against its certificate.
Preparing for the audit
Keep the certificate of magnetic strength for every separator in one file.
Keep the cleaning log, gauss readings and inspection records with it.
Mark each separator with a number that matches the file.
Make sure operators can explain the cleaning procedure and show the records.
Review the plan after any change to the line, and record the review.

Workholding Tips for Magnetic Chucks | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / Workholding Tips for Magnetic Chucks
A magnetic chuck holds best when the part is flat, clean and sits across both poles. These tips help with the jobs where that is harder to arrange.
Holding awkward parts
Most hard to hold parts have one problem in common. Only a small area touches the top plate. The aim is to give the magnetism a path into the part.
{1}Small parts.{/1} Load several parts at once, and pack steel pieces around the sides and ends for support. For thin one off parts, use a fine pole chuck. See {3}how to choose a magnetic chuck{/3}

{1}Deep or odd shaped parts.{/1} Make a simple jig from mild steel and a non-magnetic material such as brass. The mild steel carries the field up into the part. The non-magnetic layers keep the north and south paths apart. Place the jig so it sits across the poles.
{1}Repeat work.{/1} Fit an extra top plate to the chuck and shape it to the part. The part then touches a much larger area, and the chuck itself stays unmachined.

{1}Tall, thin parts.{/1} Stand two steel jaws on the chuck, one on north poles only and one on south poles only. Place the part between them. The field passes from one jaw through the part to the other, and the part is held without distortion.
Milling on a magnetic chuck
Milling puts much larger forces on a part than grinding does. The forces come in blows as each tooth strikes, and their direction keeps changing.
A chuck is best at holding a part down. It resists sliding much less well. So:
Always use side stops and end stops. Place them so the cutting force pushes the part against them.
Put packing blocks between the stops and the part, so the part stays over both a north and a south pole.
Use climb milling (down-cut milling) where the machine is built for it. The cutter pushes the part down onto the chuck, so heavier cuts can be taken.
In up-cut milling, the cutter tries to lift the part and push it along. Put the end stop against that push.
Build up feeds and cut depths slowly on a new job.
Before you start the feed, check the part, stops and packing are in place.
Installing a chuck
A chuck leaves the works ground flat and parallel. It can still be damaged in transport or handling, so check it before fitting.
A SMAG circular permanent magnetic chuck.
Check the machine table is clean, undamaged and flat.
Check the chuck base is flat.
Clean the table and the chuck base completely. One grain of dirt between them will tilt the chuck.
Fit the chuck and bolt it down.
On a grinder, grind the top plate on that machine, so it is true to that table.
On a lathe, the chuck needs a back plate. Use screws that stop short of the inside of the chuck. A screw that goes too far can jam the moving magnets.
Regrinding the top plate
Regrind the top plate when it is worn or marked. A thick top plate can be reground many times before it needs replacing.
Switch the chuck off while you regrind.
Use a medium hard wheel with an open grit.
Mounting a chuck on its side

A rectangular chuck can be mounted on edge, for example on a large angle plate. Keep the edges of the top plate and base plate from touching steel at the same time. That would short circuit the field and weaken the hold. A non-magnetic spacer at least 3 mm thick, in brass or austenitic stainless steel, prevents this.
Drilling and machining a chuck
Simple holes for locating pegs and driving pegs are fine. Follow these rules:
Never drill through into the inside of the chuck. Coolant and dirt get in, and a projection can jam the magnets.
Keep every hole at least 5 mm shallower than the plate is thick.
Drill only in the solid parts of the plate. Keep clear of the pole inserts and the spacers between them.
On a laminated fine pole top plate, keep clear of the tie rods. You can see them from the chuck ends.
Grooves or recesses cut for one job can spoil the chuck for the next. An extra top plate is usually the better choice. {1}Contact us{/1} before any larger machining.

Problem

Part will not hold
Is the part magnetic? Is it thick enough to take the field? Does it sit across at least one north and one south pole?

Side and end stops are missing or in the wrong place.
